title: The Europeans of the Indies
subtitle: Who counted as European, how many, where — c. 1600 to today
author: Ejak (Reza Arlianda), with Claude
cover: From a few hundred behind a fort wall to a quarter of a million, and then the great departure.
intro: How many Westerners lived in the Indonesian archipelago, where, and what made the number rise and fall? The answer depends on a colonial legal category, "Europeans", which covered Dutch-born newcomers (totok), a much larger group born in the Indies, and some Asians and other foreigners granted the status. This story follows the published counts, says where they differ, and uses modern provinces as stand-ins for colonial regions on the map. Sea routes that leave the frame towards the Bay of Biscay continue to the Netherlands.

slides.title: A thin layer in Batavia
slides.text: Markus Vink's census of the Dutch Indian Ocean world finds the European group in Batavia stagnant or declining. He counts 1,783 Europeans in 1699, about 8 per cent of the city, then 1,541 in 1749 and only 478 in 1797. Jean Gelman Taylor presents Batavia as a trading base that grew into the centre of the Dutch Asian empire, where Europeans and Asians changed one another.
slides.more: Vink's tables separate "Europeans" from "mixed peoples" but never define either. Batavia's surrounding districts (Ommelanden) held only 600–800 Europeans and mestizos together. Vink counts settlements, not the whole VOC world, and gives no grand total of Europeans.

slides.title: Garrisons in the spice islands
slides.text: Vink's figures show how small the European presence was even at key forts. Ternate had 680 Dutch in 1682, over a third of its residents, but Makassar counted only 69 Europeans in 1676. Ambon fell from 928 Europeans in 1740 to 319 by 1780, and Banda held 153 in 1787. These are single settlements, not totals for the colony.
slides.more: At Makassar in 1730 Vink combines Europeans and mixed people in one figure, 622, about 12 per cent of the town. Where the two are merged, he marks the table, so such figures cannot be compared directly with the Europeans-only ones above.

slides.label: 1600s–1800s
slides.title: A mixed society
slides.text: Few European women travelled to the Indies, so many men formed families with Asian women. Laarman reports 220 European women per 1,000 men in 1632, against 884 in 1930. Taylor argues this produced a hybrid Indo-Dutch culture. Bosma and Raben are reported to say Indos made up almost 80 per cent of "Europeans", but their reviewer notes that this counts creoles broadly.
slides.more: Bosma and Raben trace "creolisation" from 1500 to 1920. Van der Veur criticises some of their claims, for example about European women in the seventeenth century. Laarman adds that 20–25 per cent of European marriages in the late colony were mixed (p. 51).

slides.label: 1814–c. 1860
slides.title: Few Europeans, mostly men
slides.text: Van Imhoff and Beets cite a count of about 2,000 Europeans on Java and Madura in 1814, not counting the military. A NIDI demographic report notes around 22,000 European men but fewer than 1,000 European women near 1860. Van der Veur, reviewing Bosma and Raben, summarises the story: Java's European population stayed minimal and grew only after the 1860s.
slides.more: The NIDI passage consulted does not say exactly which group the 1860 figures cover, so treat the male-female contrast as a rough picture of a transient, male-dominated community rather than a precise census.

slides.title: Who counted as European?
slides.text: Colonial law, set out in article 109 of the 1854 constitution, split Europeans from everyone else, and let the state move individuals across the line. Japanese residents gained European status in 1899. By 1930 the category held Dutch totok, Indies-born Indos, other Westerners, Japanese, Filipinos, Armenians, Turks, Egyptians and some Indonesians given equal status. A child recognised by a European father took his status.
slides.more: Van der Veur reports 7,195 Japanese and 542 Armenians among the 1930 Europeans, plus about 9,000 Indonesians who became Europeans by decree. Locher-Scholten calls the three-way legal split (Europeans, Foreign Orientals, natives) a form of legal apartheid.

slides.title: The Suez shortcut
slides.text: Locher-Scholten notes that after the Suez Canal opened in 1869, connections with Europe improved greatly, and the colony grew more attractive to Dutch newcomers. Pelzer's study of East Sumatra shows the colonial government using the 1870 Agrarian Law to hand land to European planters. No verified European counts for 1870–1900 were found, so this slide gives the cause, not a number.
slides.more: Counts for Java and Madura in 1880, 1890 and 1900 circulate online, citing Wiseman 2000; that source has not been checked yet, so they are left out.

slides.title: The Deli plantation belt
slides.text: Pelzer dates the Deli planting boom to 1863, when Nienhuys arrived, followed by Swiss and German planters in 1865–66. The government moved its seat to Medan in 1887. In 1930, Pelzer's table counts about 11,000 Europeans in East Sumatra: 0.7 per cent of 1.5 million people, but 5 per cent of Medan. Stoler's study covers this plantation belt from 1870.

slides.title: Totok families and a "tropical Netherlands"
slides.text: Locher-Scholten finds the totok population of Java and Madura more than doubled between 1905 and 1930. European-born women there rose from about 4,000 to 26,000, and European women per 1,000 men climbed from 471 in 1880 to 884 in 1930. A later passage describes totokisation: better health, schools and sport made temporary stays easier, and a tropical Netherlands took shape.

slides.title: The count
slides.text: The colonial census of 7 October 1930 counted 240,417 Europeans among 60.7 million people, 0.4 per cent. The NIDI report derived 86.7 per cent Dutch nationals from it (208,269 people). Of those, 73.9 per cent were born in the Indies and 25.8 per cent in the Netherlands. The 1920 census gave about 170,000 Europeans, though Van Imhoff and Beets call it experimental.
slides.more: Totals differ slightly: 240,162 for age and sex tables, about 243,000 with ship crews (NIDI), and 246,000 in Van Imhoff and Beets's Journal of Population Research article (p. 53). Locher-Scholten and Van Imhoff and Beets round to 240,000.

slides.title: Where they lived
slides.text: Locher-Scholten says four-fifths of Europeans lived on Java. Castles, working from the census, counts 37,076 Europeans in Batavia with Meester Cornelis, out of 533,015 people; about 33,000 of them held Dutch nationality. In East Sumatra Pelzer finds around 11,000. Verified 1930 counts for Bandung, Semarang and Surabaya are still to be found, so they carry no numbers.

slides.title: Camps
slides.text: NIOD puts the pre-war European population near 290,000, with about 260,000 Dutch nationals; NIDI's model gives 294,000 to 305,000 in January 1942. Japanese forces held about 42,000 Dutch navy and KNIL prisoners and about 100,000 civilians. NIOD cites civilian camp deaths of 10,580 to 16,800 and 8,200 prisoner-of-war deaths; Bosma gives 10 per cent of civilians and 23 per cent of prisoners.
slides.more: De Jong's regional table totals 96,400 internees; a Japanese report to the Red Cross gave about 98,000 and a postwar Dutch statement about 110,000. NIOD calls about 100,000 the most reliable estimate.

sources.cite: NIOD Institute for War n.d., page on occupation numbers

slides.title: Outside the wire
slides.text: Not every European was behind barbed wire. NIOD estimates 120,000 to 200,000 stayed outside the camps, and cites Hans Meijer at about 125,000. Bosma, in the introduction to his volume, says half the Dutch population in Indonesia was interned and elsewhere that most Europeans were concentrated in detention camps. The gap partly reflects who counts as Dutch, and the sources I read do not break this group down further.

sources.cite: NIOD Institute for War n.d., page on occupation numbers

slides.title: Bersiap
slides.text: After Japan's surrender, violence against Europeans, Indo-Europeans and others swept Java and Sumatra. Estimates conflict. NIDI's demographic model assumes about 3,500 extra deaths; Van den Berge, citing Frederick, reports 25,000–30,000 Dutch and Indo-European civilian casualties. Captain and Sinke record local incidents and say about 46,000 people, 4,500 of them totok, were held in 398 camps on Java and Madura.
slides.more: The two headline figures may measure different things: a modelled death surplus versus total casualties. Captain and Sinke's victim-estimates chapter was not read.

slides.title: Evacuation and the offensives
slides.text: Van Imhoff and Beets place the first departure wave directly after the war. The NIDI report, citing Bossenbroek, says almost 110,000 people were taken from the Indies to the Netherlands between 1945 and 1948, and about half stayed. Meanwhile Laarman reports about 95,000 Dutch conscripts fought in the Indies after the war, during the offensives of 1947 and 1948.

sources.cite: Bosma 2012, ch. 3 (Laarman), p. 61; ch. 2 (Jones), p. 46 n. 3

slides.title: Sovereignty and the choice of nationality
slides.text: The 1949 separation agreement gave Dutch nationality to Dutch and Indies-born Europeans, and Indonesian nationality to non-European Dutch subjects, according to NIDI. Van Imhoff and Beets subtract about 6,000 people who chose Indonesian nationality permanently, and name independence in 1949 as the second migration wave. Bosma notes that about 90 per cent of immigrants from Indonesia had been classed as Europeans in colonial times.

slides.title: The Moluccan soldiers
slides.text: Moluccan soldiers of the colonial army were not Westerners, but they travelled in the same exodus. About 12,500 people arrived in 1951 (NIDI): 3,578 former KNIL soldiers and 574 other men, plus family. Bosma gives about 4,000 soldiers and 8,000 wives and children. Most had given up Indonesian nationality by about 1958 and were stateless; only 1,758 returned to Indonesia between 1951 and 1970.
slides.more: Jones describes these Moluccans as former soldiers housed in temporary camps. Their number is already part of the larger total of about 312,500 migrants in her chapter, shown on a later slide.

slides.title: "Black Sinterklaas"
slides.text: Amid the West New Guinea dispute, 5 December 1957 became known as the day of the Black Sinterklaas. Delfos writes that Dutch people were declared a danger to the state and asked to leave, and Dutch companies were nationalised. Bosma says Indonesia declared Dutch citizens personae non gratae. Van Imhoff and Beets count 1958, when the remaining Dutch had to take Indonesian nationality or leave, as the third wave. None of these sources gives a figure for 1957–58 alone.

slides.title: Counting the departures
slides.text: Totals differ with who is counted and which years. Van Imhoff and Beets estimate 254,000 Dutch persons left between 1946 and 1967. Bosma writes of almost 300,000 Dutch citizens between 1945 and 1962. Jones gives about 312,500 in the 1950s and 1960s: roughly 200,000 Indo-Dutch, 12,500 Moluccans and 100,000 "white" Dutch. Delfos reports about 13,000 spijtoptanten, who regretted choosing Indonesian citizenship, left within two years after 1960.

slides.title: New Guinea changes hands
slides.text: The Netherlands and Indonesia signed the New York Agreement in August 1962. Saltford records that a UN authority took over from the Dutch on 1 October 1962 and handed the territory to Indonesia on 1 May 1963. NIDI notes about 300 Moluccans reached the Netherlands from New Guinea after the transfer. No verified count of Dutch officials and residents leaving has been found, so none is shown.

slides.title: Afterlives
slides.text: Van Imhoff and Beets reconstruct 582,000 Indo-Dutch on 1 January 2001, counting the second generation: 458,000 in the Netherlands and 124,000 elsewhere. The total peaked at about 616,000 in 1984, with a margin of error near 10 per cent. The group is wider than the colonial category, covering European, Asian and mixed descent. In 1930 The Hague already had the largest concentration of Indies-born Dutch. None of the sources I read gives a count of Westerners in Indonesia today.
